items.article_context_en: Speaking at Ripple's conference, the U.S. Treasury Secretary said the SEC and CFTC action could help fill the gap left by the Clarity Act's failure, while curbing crypto debanking. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said digital assets could help strengthen the U.S. dollar's global dominance as technology becomes an increasingly important source of American economic influence. Speaking Tuesday at Ripple's Swell conference with CEO Brad Garlinghouse, Bessent argued that the power behind the world's reserve currencies during history derived from military strength, but it’s increasingly shifting toward technological leadership. "We will keep our military umbrella, but I think more and more it's becoming a technology umbrella," Bessent said. He pointed to the growing divide between U.S. and Chinese technology ecosystems, where countries and companies face choices over whose artificial intelligence systems and semiconductor technology to adopt. Bessent said he sees digital assets as part of that competition, with the financial infrastructure countries may choose influencing the U.S. "I think that digital assets are going to be no different, and we are going to win in the digital asset stack, and that's gonna continue to fortify the [U.S.] dollar," he said. His remarks offered a broader rationale for the administration of President Donald Trump’s push to bring crypto businesses onshore, framing digital assets not just as a financial market but as part of the infrastructure that could sustain U.S. The administration has already secured passage of the GENIUS Act, which established a federal regulatory framework for stablecoins, cryptocurrencies designed to maintain a fixed value against fiat currencies like the U.S. Bessent argued that stablecoins could reinforce the dollar's position by expanding access to U.S. currency in countries where local currencies face inflation or sharp swings in value.

items.article_context_en: Crypto trading volume fell 38% from year-ago levels, but the firm's overall blockchain business gained traction. Crypto transaction revenue dropped to $120 million in the third quarter, according to the company's earnings report released Tuesday. That was down from about $267 million in the same period last year, but ahead of Wall Street analysts’ expectations of $114.1 million. That left crypto accounting for just 8.4% of Robinhood's $1.42 billion in total quarterly revenue, compared with roughly 21% a year earlier. The decline came as customers traded less crypto across Robinhood's platforms. Total crypto trading volume fell 38% to $50 billion, including $21 billion through the Robinhood app, down 48%, and $29 billion through crypto exchange Bitstamp, down 28%. The slump in crypto trading revenue stood in contrast to Robinhood's broader business. Total revenue rose 12% year-over-year to $1.424 billion, helped by growth in options, equities and prediction markets. Street estimates had been for $1.43 billion. Options trading generated $399 million in revenue, up 31%, while equities revenue climbed 41% to $121 million. Prediction markets brought in $173 million, more than six times the year-earlier figure. Third-quarter EPS of $0.51 was less than consensus forecasts for $0.55. Despite weaker crypto trading, Robinhood continued to build out its digital asset business. The company said Robinhood Chain, its blockchain network, processed more than $80 billion in decentralized exchange trading volume and generated over $50 million in chain fees during its first quarter operating on mainnet.

items.article_context_en: USDT volume on MB jumped nearly 800% and bitcoin 865% from the previous Sunday; Binance’s USDT/BRL market rose 251% while its global BTC/USDT pair fell. Brazilian companies entered a crypto trading frenzy on Sunday to protect their treasuries from the outcome of an election that saw incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, unexpectedly beat Flávio Bolsonaro. Corporate accounts generated 78% of trading on crypto exchange Mercado Bitcoin, with turnover in Tether’s dollar-pegged stablecoin, USDT, jumping nearly 800% from the week before and more than triple the average of the four preceding Sundays. Trading in bitcoin BTC$84,459.46 surged 865% compared with the previous Sunday, the exchange said. Lula’s platform of increased social spending and a ban on online betting that would reduce tax income sparked concerns the country’s finances would suffer if he won, adding to pressure on the real and keeping borrowing costs high. Rising debt, new spending commitments and limited scope for tax increases would make that task harder. “For investors, this reinforces the logic of not relying only on the real,” Pedro Fontes, a research analyst at Mercado Bitcoin, wrote in an analysis shared with CoinDesk. “In this scenario of higher exchange rate pressure, stablecoins, such as USDT and USDC, are a simple way to dollarize part of your assets, at any time and starting from low amounts.” Stronger opposition in Congress could complicate efforts to address fiscal problems, reinforcing the appeal of assets whose prices are set in global markets, he said. Corporate concerns materialized the next day, when the benchmark Ibovespa stock index crashed 14% in its worst performance since March 2020 and the dollar jumped more than 8% against the real, its largest daily gain since 1999. The response had been different three weeks earlier, when Bolsonaro finished ahead of Lula in the first round of voting. The Ibovespa jumped 7.7% and the dollar weakened more than 4% against the real as investors anticipated a change of government and tighter control over public spending. Lula´s victory made him the first presidential candidate in Brazil’s modern democracy to secure a victory after finishing in second place. Even so, Brazil’s companies took a cautious stance. “The main driver of volume was companies seeking to protect their treasuries,” Mercado Bitcoin said.

items.article_context_en: Luxor is building price indexes and future contracts for compute power, adapting its Bitcoin hashprice derivative model for AI workloads. Bitcoin mining companies are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI), renting out computing power and converting mining facilities into data centers. Now, some of the companies that built their businesses serving bitcoin miners are following them into the AI market. Luxor Technology, best known for its bitcoin mining services, is also moving into AI hardware and trading contracts that allow companies to agree on computing prices in advance. The Seattle-based company said on Tuesday that it raised $16 million in a round led by CMT Digital. Bitcoin mining equipment makers Canaan and MicroBT also invested. Luxor said the money will go toward its AI hardware brokerage and computing-power trading business. The round included new investment and sales of existing shares, although Luxor did not disclose how much of the new funding was invested in the company. Publicly traded bitcoin miners had signed more than $70 billion worth of AI and high-performance computing contracts by the end of March, according to CoinShares data. Not everyone is moving away from bitcoin mining. Nasdaq-listed NIP Group (NIPG) announced plans last week to essentially increase its mining capacity by about 48%. The company said it expects to generate about 195 bitcoin a month at full deployment. Moving into AI also requires more than access to electricity. Ethan Vera, Luxor's chief operating officer, told CoinDesk that its software business works with bitcoin miners representing nearly two gigawatts of power capacity.

Bitcoin BTC$84,459.46 slipped below $80,000 on Tuesday, dropping 0.4% since midnight UTC to near $79,700. Altcoins fell further, with ether ETH$2,490.55, the largest, losing 0.5%. The DeFi index (DFX) dropped 1.8%, the most of any CoinDesk index, a reversal from Monday, when it was the only index to gain. stock index futures edged lower ahead of big-tech earnings later this week. Asian tech shares rallied, with South Korea’s Kospi rising 3.1%, though the advance didn’t pull crypto along with it. items.article_context_en: The breach exposed 25,964 buyer records, some kept past Keystone’s 180-day deletion policy after an automated tool failed without the firm noticing. An attacker gained access to the company’s website on Oct. 20 through a flaw in a third-party data monitoring tool, Keystone said Monday in a post on X. The attack exposed 25,964 buyer records from 2024 through 2026, including names, contact details, shipping addresses and order information. Another 12,873 unpaid checkout records may have been affected. The breach adds to a string of attacks on hardware wallet users this year. At Ledger, criminals fitted devices sold through resellers in Southeast Asia, with hidden components capturing recovery phrases during setup. Similarly, a flaw in Coldcard’s seed-generation software let attackers reconstruct private keys and drain wallets remotely. The stolen Keystone key is built into devices during production and cannot be changed. It allows wallets to pass online authenticity checks, raising the risk that fake devices could appear genuine and put users' funds at risk, according to the firm. The company said it will destroy 18,835 unsold units. Keystone said the breach did not expose recovery phrases, private keys or wallet credentials. Some customer records should have been deleted under Keystone's 180-day retention policy, but an automated deletion tool failed without the company detecting the issue, it said. “We failed to fulfill our commitment to erase customer data on time, and we accept responsibility for this failure,” Keystone wrote.
